components.text: Madhubani: look for a surface packed edge to edge with pattern, bold outlines, double-line borders, and symbolic motifs like fish, birds, lotuses, and deity figures.
Warli: look for a restrained palette, usually white on brown, with stick-like human figures built from circles and triangles, often arranged in circles around dances or work scenes.

Pattachitra: look for smooth, highly detailed composition, stylized faces with large eyes, decorative borders, mythological storytelling, and a painted surface that often resembles a prepared cloth scroll.
Madhubani is closely tied to domestic ritual, marriage, fertility, and seasonal festivals, which is why its imagery often feels intimate and ceremonial.
Warli documents lived community practice: work, celebration, and collective identity, usually through a very spare visual language.
Pattachitra serves as a visual vehicle for religious narration, especially around Jagannath devotion and epic stories.
Ask whether the artist signs the work, where it was made, and how it was produced; genuine practitioners usually welcome questions about process and cultural background.

Buy from recognized artisan communities and makers who can identify their village or lineage, such as Mithila artists for Madhubani, Warli artists from Maharashtra’s tribal belt, and Chitrakar/Pattachitra practitioners in Odisha and Bengal.
Prefer works made with traditional methods and materials when available: natural pigments, hand-prepared surfaces, and hand-drawn outlines rather than mass-printed reproductions.

Purchase through artisan cooperatives, museum shops, craft fairs, or verified platforms that document the maker and locality; current reliable market data on individual artists is limited, so provenance matters more than brand names.
Avoid pricing that undercuts handmade labor; fair payment helps keep these traditions viable across generations.

tradition_data.origins: Mithila region of Bihar, especially Madhubani, Darbhanga, and Sitamarhi
tradition_data.materials: Traditionally mud walls; now paper, cloth, and canvas; natural dyes, twigs/fingers/matchsticks
tradition_data.motifs: Deities, wedding/fertility symbols, fish, birds, flowers, nature, village life
tradition_data.technique: Dense line work, geometric filling, no empty space, bold borders
tradition_data.context: Traditionally painted by women for rituals, festivals, and auspicious occasions

tradition_data.origins: Tribal communities of Maharashtra, especially northern Konkan and districts such as Thane and Palghar
tradition_data.materials: Mud walls or earthen surfaces; white rice paste with water/gum; often a red-brown ground
tradition_data.motifs: Daily village life, farming, hunting, dance, marriage, harvest, animals
tradition_data.technique: Minimalist white geometric figures made from circles, triangles, and lines
tradition_data.context: Linked to community life and social rituals rather than deity-centered storytelling

tradition_data.origins: Odisha, especially around Puri and Raghurajpur, and also parts of West Bengal
tradition_data.materials: Cloth or palm leaf; prepared cloth base with chalk/gum; natural pigments and fine brushes
tradition_data.motifs: Jagannath, Krishna, Rama, Mahabharata/Ramayana scenes, mythological narratives
tradition_data.technique: Fine outlines, intricate narrative panels, strong borders, tightly composed figures
tradition_data.context: Devotional and temple-linked art connected to Jagannath culture and ritual storytelling
